workloads.name: SAXPY (vector update)
workloads.what: Updates a long vector with y = a·x + y: almost pure memory traffic.

peak: Memory: 8 channels x DDR5-4800 x 8 B = 307.2 GB/s
measured: Measured memory limit: 214 GB/s (70% of theory)
header.achieved: At sizes larger than the cache: 197 GB/s to 238 GB/s (64–77% of the theoretical limit); best at vector length 16M, fp64.
why: Each element is read and written once with almost no arithmetic, so memory speed sets the limit; sizes that fit in the cache can run faster than memory allows.
The memory limit here is the pure-read speed: this processor skips the usual extra read when it writes whole cache lines.

workloads.name: Image convolution
workloads.what: Slides a small filter over a large image, as in image processing.

peak: Compute: 28 cores × 3.0 GHz (the highest clock the processor reached while running matrix multiply; Intel does not publish an all-core AVX-512 clock) × 32 fp64 FLOP/cycle (2 AVX-512 FMA units) = 2.69 TFLOP/s fp64; fp32 = 2×

header.achieved: Reached 4,677 Mpixels/s to 61,159 Mpixels/s across sizes (7–26% of the theoretical limit); best at image size 1K, 1 channel, 3×3 filter.
why: Small filters do little arithmetic per pixel, so only part of the compute limit is reachable; larger filters do more work per pixel and get closer.
Our own hand-written kernel is the fastest at almost every size on every machine: general-purpose neural-network libraries are not built for one small filter over a large image.
